summary: Considers deficiencies of the 1988 X.500 standard that need to be addressed before an effective open Internet Directory can be built, focusing on replication. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A big shared phone book needs copies in many places. This lists what is missing to make that work.

subtitle: Making a global directory work by replicating data widely.

tldr.problem: The 1988 X.500 directory standard lacks replication, making it unsuitable for a scalable Internet directory.
tldr.mechanism: Replication of directory knowledge and data across multiple servers enables both responsiveness and availability.
tldr.outcome: The RFC identifies five critical replication requirements that any Internet directory must address before deployment.

today: RFC 1275 is an informational document examining design gaps in X.500. While X.500 saw some deployment as a research project, it did not become the Internet's directory system. LDAP, based on X.500 but simpler, became the standard directory protocol for the Internet and is widely deployed today.

sections.title: Introduction to X.500 and the Internet Directory
sections.content: RFC 1275 examines deficiencies in the 1988 X.500 standard that must be solved before it can serve as an Internet directory. X.500 defines a distributed directory system using Directory Service Agents (DSAs) that answer directory queries. The RFC focuses on replication, the practice of maintaining copies of directory data on multiple servers. Without replication, a single server becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
sections.eli5: When many people need to look up a phone number at the same time, one person answering the phone can only handle so many calls. You need more people answering phones in different places.

sections.title: Knowledge Replication
sections.content: Directory servers must know how to route queries to the right place. This routing information is called knowledge. Knowledge about the top of the directory tree must be replicated widely. Consider resolving a name under Country=US; a DSA needs complete knowledge of that subtree. Many DSAs must have this knowledge to provide fast, reliable response. Requiring all queries to go through one server would be an unacceptable bottleneck.
sections.eli5: Imagine a post office where letters need to be routed to the right town. The main post office needs to know where every town is, and so do many other post offices.

sections.title: Data Replication for Search
sections.content: Many searches happen at the root and country level, such as approximate matching of organization names. X.500's standard approach of subordinate references (pointers to entries held in other DSAs) makes such searches inefficient. Instead, data must be replicated where people search for it most. Replication is particularly important high in the directory tree and between different implementations. At lower levels, DSAs from the same vendor can use implementation-specific techniques.
sections.eli5: If you look up "United States" in a phone book, the book should have that information right there, not just a note saying "ask this other book."

sections.title: Availability and Scaling
sections.content: When a DSA returns a referral, it indicates only one master server. This creates a single point of failure. Additional references to slave copies must be allowed to improve availability. The RFC calls for deployment guidelines and defines scaling targets: the pilot was envisioned to handle approximately 100,000 non-leaf entries and several million leaf entries. Replication mechanisms must not exceed the scaling limits of the technique used.
sections.eli5: If the main server is broken, a request can go to a backup copy. And the system needs to keep working even with a million names.

references.text: Rose, M. and D. Cass, "ISO Transport Services on top of the TCP", RFC 1006, May 1987.
